Apple has accused a new UK proposal targeting App Store fees of amounting to price control today, warning that such a move could harm innovation and investment. Here are the details.

Apple Opposes App Store Regulation in the UK

According to a report by Reuters, Apple today filed a formal submission in response to a consultation by the UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), opposing a proposed rule that would allow app developers to link to alternative payment options.

The CMA was granted the authority to impose such rules last year after designating Apple and Google as having "strategic market status" in their respective mobile platform markets. Under the UK's new digital markets regime, this designation allows the regulator to introduce company-specific rules aimed at promoting competition and offering consumers more choice.

Under the proposal, Apple and Google could still charge commissions on transactions completed via alternative payment methods, but any associated fees must be deemed "fair and reasonable."

Reuters noted that the CMA "expects that the cost of steering will be lower than current App Store charges, and that the savings will be passed on to UK consumers or reinvested in developers' businesses to support innovation."

Apple, however, sees things differently and has objected to the proposal. Here is Reuters' report:

The CMA has rejected Apple's characterisation of the proposal as price control, stating that its aim is to set principles for determining whether steering fees are fair and reasonable, rather than directly setting fee levels.
